A set is identifiable through a ratio $p/q$ if its characteristic vector is uniquely determined by the vector of ratios into which its elements are divided by a given ratio $p/q$. We establish that a set $S$ is identifiable through a ratio $p/q$ if and only if there exists a bijection $\phi$ that partitions its elements based on their structure in the network and maps them into distinct intervals so that elements within the same connected component of the network's subgraph induced by $S$ are integrated into the same interval under $\phi$.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the differential decay rate of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ transition is determined. This decay process is analyzed in terms of hadron momenta, retraced to the quark and lepton momenta at the time of the decay, with which the decay rate's underlying physics is uncovered. A precise measurement of the decay rate is achieved in two-dimensional bins of lepton and hadron energies, as well as a measurement of the average decay length of $B_s^0$ mesons. Theoretical predictions are compared to experimental results for the decay rate, with which the angular integral of the decay rate is determined. A precise measurement of the decay rate's form is also achieved, which is crucial for the precise calculation of semileptonic $B$ decay rates in the standard model and beyond.

A persistent mystery in acoustic emission signals from cracking materials has been resolved by our findings, who uncovered a direct connection between tape deformation and sound generation. Through a combination of theoretical analysis, laboratory experiments and a newly developed model, we discovered that peeling forces primarily influence sound production by altering contact pressures between the tape and surface, rather than simply being triggered by cracks. This insight contradicts a widely accepted assumption that acoustic emission signals directly reflect crack growth, and may have important implications for interpreting similar signals in other materials.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Our proposed framework, TPC, is designed to enhance point cloud models by applying a novel diffusion-based learning process that incorporates a unique transformation module. Our findings reveal that our method consistently outperforms existing techniques, specifically RDS, in terms of precision, with noticeable improvements observed in our experiments. Our proposed method also demonstrates a significant advantage over RDS in terms of parameter efficiency. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghou-q/TPC.

The process of testing programs has become increasingly complex, and the tools used to aid this process also grow more complicated. Despite the growing number of programs and their complexity, the amount of testing that takes place has not kept pace, and therefore, new methods of testing are necessary. This paper introduces a novel approach to testing based on the concepts of coverage and the geometry of the programs being tested. A graphical model represents the possible executions of a program, with areas corresponding to different outcomes and types of errors. An optimal testing strategy is achieved by filling this graphical area in a specific, most efficient manner, with the least amount of testing required to cover all possible scenarios and detect various types of errors.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of the conjecture proposed by Grothendieck, relating to the description of local components of representations of the algebraic fundamental group for curves over p-adic fields, specifically for curves of genus 1. Our argument revolves around the application of relative Kummer theory in an abelian variety, which enables us to identify and describe certain components of these representations. In the process, we derive clear information about the weights of these components, which serves as the primary contribution of our work.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate sensing capabilities into damaged areas of structures are a promising development in damage detection technology. This study proposes a novel method, Exact Damage Shaping, which utilizes genetic algorithms in conjunction with real-time data from electrical impedance tomography (EIT) to accurately determine the optimal placement of heat or mechanical stress that compensates for defects within self-sensing composite structures. A key advantage of this approach is the exact reconstruction of damage profiles, as proven by multiple test scenarios featuring various injury configurations. As a result, a complex damage pattern consisting of two distinct defects is successfully mapped and pinpointed through a fair but challenging distribution of stressing points. These findings demonstrate the capability of Exact Damage Shaping in accurately identifying damage in composite structures with real-time EIT feedback and genetically optimized stress distribution.

This work presents a tensor approach to a Euclidean space of any finite dimension, utilizing geometric vector quantities. A comprehensive overview of this method is provided, detailing the key aspects of the vector algebra used in this tensor description.

A right-angled Artin group (RAG) can be viewed as the fundamental group of a chamber system, consisting of a collection of polygons linked at their edges. We examine the structure of this chamber system when each polygon is replaced by a tree, which results in a right-angled Artin graph. Conversely, when the graph is simple and connected, we demonstrate that the associated RAG acts transitively on the edges of the tree-like chamber system, which in turn is equivalent to the RAG being hyperbolic.

The development of GPU-accelerated algorithms for matrix inversion has been hindered by the current techniques, which are largely based on first-order iterative methods such as Newton-Raphson and Broyden. This holdback occurs due to the limited utilization of higher-order methods that could provide a performance boost from GPUs. This research addresses this gap by introducing higher-order iterative methods that are suitable for GPU acceleration and examining their performance in comparison to existing techniques. A key contribution of this study involves the creation of a higher-order iterative algorithm that combines the advantages of Salstein and Broyden methods and exceeds their performance in various benchmark tests. Additionally, the research explores the development of higher-order methods that utilize a preconditioning matrix and identifies an optimal condition for this purpose. The findings of this study provide a foundation for the design of high-performance GPU algorithms for solving large-scale linear systems and could have significant implications for various numerical applications, especially those involving sparse matrices, as well as advances in linear algebra software and packages.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred following the advent of decentralized learning techniques such as Federated Learning. As a result, there's a growing need to explore contextual linear bandits in settings where data is distributed and privacy is a pressing concern. This paper presents an innovative, context-aware, linear-bandit learning algorithm that doesn't require sharing the context. This algorithm uses a few updates of a context-independent model to approximate the optimal action for each context. This approach has several benefits over other methods that also avoid sharing the context, due to its ability to handle a wide range of context dimensions and yield nearly optimal regret bounds.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion is also known to negatively impact VSI stability. This paper investigates the potential influences of particle growth and settling on VSI stability in distant disk sections, taking into account various particle properties and cooling methods. The results show that VSI instability is more difficult to maintain in areas with larger particle sizes and those that have settled lower due to gravity, although it can still occur in regions with sufficient gas turbulence or in areas with shorter cooling times. Consequently, VSI stability varies significantly across different radial and height locations within the same disk system, leading to a diverse range of turbulent patterns and dust development/settling outcomes in different areas.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in deep learning have been compromised by the emergence of convolutional neural network (CNN) backdoors, which are crafted by adding subtle modifications to incoming data and injecting a hidden command. In response, research has focused on detecting backdoors in CNN models, particularly in image classification tasks. Existing detection methods have been successful; however, they rely on assumptions that the backdoored layer is fixed and noticeable. In contrast, our research investigates dynamic backdoors that are triggered by specific input characteristics, which cannot be pinpointed in advance. Such backdoors complicate detection as they are activated and deactivated continuously. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel detection technique using global mean pooling layers, which are commonly found in CNN architectures. Our method, called DB-GMP, exploits the fact that global mean pooling disables dynamic backdoors by reducing them to a constant value. The effectiveness of DB-GMP is demonstrated through experiments on three different datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TNIST), which reveals that our technique outperforms existing methods in all cases. Consequently, we believe that our findings have significant implications for ensuring the security and trustworthiness of CNN models in various applications.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores an innovative algorithm called Stroll for Addressing these issues. This algorithm utilizes a random walk technique to construct a representative graph of data distribution, differing from existing methods that rely on explicit connectivity information or assume a predefined graph structure. A thorough analysis of the algorithm's convergence properties reveals that Stroll achieves an almost linear reduction in communication costs, compared to other random walk-based algorithms. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the efficacy of Stroll in real-world scenarios by conducting experiments on various data sets and comparing its performance to other notable algorithms.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining a consistency objective between annotated and anonymously labelled images with a modified adversarial loss to enhance semi-supervised segmentation models. The key advantage of this method is that it eliminates the need for anonymously labelled data, differing from similar approaches that utilize noise or adversarial regularization. The proposed technique has several benefits over existing methods, primarily due to its simplicity and the absence of complicated optimization processes. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this new method outperforms numerous semi-supervised and unsupervised segmentation techniques, further illustrating its effectiveness.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-based Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-FL approaches that address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

A recurrent neural network like LSTMs has numerous applications in natural language processing, speech recognition, and currently video identification, which makes it a highly sought-after model. However, its size can be quite substantial, leading to prolonged training times and decreased use in embedded devices due to power constraints. This paper addresses the above issues by presenting a combined algorithm and hardware design for an energy-efficient long short-term memory network, targeting specific memory access patterns to minimize data movement and optimizing the neural network structure to utilize existing hardware features efficiently. A hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition was also employed to reduce model size and improve memory usage. Experimental results showed that the proposed hierarchy-based tensor decomposition outperformed existing methods in both accuracy and model size, with a 23.5 times increase in memory access efficiency and a 2.5 times decrease in model size on a popular video identification dataset, and the designed hardware achieved a 12 times improvement in throughput compared to a state-of-the-art FPGA.

A positive integer is prime if its only positive divisors are 1 and itself. We offer a characterization of prime numbers based on the behavior of polynomial compositions and their iterates, specifically in the variable x, when we consider mappings like f(x) = P(x^d), where a positive integer results from an integer polynomial with integer coefficients when we evaluate the (n+1)th iterate at a value from a set in the complex numbers.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions exponentially blow up within a finite time period cannot occur. Additionally, we derive an upper bound on the $H^1$ norm of solutions at some given time, which is invariant under the equation's flow. These findings contribute to our understanding of the equation's dynamic properties in a given context.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over a finitely generated rational algebra have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical principles and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various computational approaches and the resulting issues with Bayes factor estimates, including the reliability of bridge sampling and the limitations of numerical methods. We also examine the instability of Bayes factor changes in relation to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws and the variable performance of different MCMC algorithms. Additionally, we discuss the drawbacks of Bayes factors in assessing complex scientific hypotheses and the advantages of integrating analysis of evidence with other aspects of theory evaluation. We conclude that Bayes factor analysis is a potentially unreliable method for evaluating scientific theories due to its dependence on questionable assumptions and the limitations of available computational tools. We suggest that researchers consider the statistical underpinnings of Bayes factor analysis and the need for a utilitarian approach that prioritizes the validation of underlying models over Bayes factor estimates.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate how discourse indicators contribute to the representation of sentences in classification tasks. Existing studies have established correlations between discourse indicators and sentence representations but are limited to specific instances and indicators. In contrast, discourse indicators vary greatly and their relationships are complex. To rectify this, the paper utilizes existing classification models to predict discourse indicators between sentences with established semantic links in multiple datasets and examines the underlying mechanisms of discourse indicators in sentence representations. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the roles discourse indicators play in capturing semantic connections between sentences.

We present a one-parameter extension of the Jordanian twistor, which is termed the extended Jordanian twistor. Our construction involves the underlying underlying structure of the underlying structure of the underlying structure, specifically the Hecke algebra. The extended Jordanian twistor arises as a natural generator, alongside its companions, within the free associative algebra. We identify the Rota-Baxter operator associated with the extended Jordanian twistor, as well as its (co)centre. Furthermore, we derive the (co)centre of the extended Jordanian twistor in the classical limit, which resembles the centre of the extended Jordanian twistor in the classical limit.

This research develops an innovative method for resolving extended regular expression-based constraints, expanding the traditional regular expressions with their combining operators and the regular expression distance metric. A polynomial-time algorithm was created to determine whether there's a difference in the formed regular expressions, building upon the existing technique by Aluru for comparing regular expressions. The novel approach splits the problem into more manageable parts by applying the ACKY regular expression syntax production rules in reverse, distinct from similar methods that digest the given regular expressions. This distinctive characteristic allows the research to extend the traditional regular expression theory to incorporate new operators, assess the satisfiability of queries regarding the regular expression distance, and explore various applications in software verification, particularly in analyzing reachability conditions for regular expression-based models.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which results in the representation of conserved current conformal block operators in CFT$_2$ in terms of geodesic operators defined within the AdS$_2$ framework rather than the AdS$_3$ framework. Moreover, this new perspective enables a direct link between the AdS$_2$ geodesic operator representation and massless higher-spin fields in the AdS$_3$ framework, facilitated by the HKLL bulk field reconstruction method. By harnessing this new picture, we are able to derive a closed-form expression for the four-point conformal block involving spinning primary fields as a product of two AdS$_2$ geodesic Witten diagrams.

To achieve high-resolution imaging with wide-field X-ray telescopes, a common issue arises from the limited number of degrees of output angle that mirror substrates can be fabricated to meet the curved shape of lobster-eye optics, which roughly corresponds to 20. Overcoming this constraint is the focus of the presented research. A novel concept involving the use of multiple lobster-eye optics with different curvature values is introduced and analyzed. The study finds that in a two-times-two array configuration, each optics can be designed to cover a 10x10 arcmin field of view, resulting in four separate fields of view, each with a resolution of approximately 10 arcsec. Theoretical performance calculations indicate that each optics can be optimized to focus X-rays within a specific energy range, allaying concerns about competition between different optics for the same focal point. The research suggests that multiple lobster-eye optics with varying curvature values can be used to achieve high-resolution imaging across a wide field of view, potentially enabling the development of wide-field X-ray monitoring systems with high sensitivity for detecting transient events.

To investigate the relationship between the cosmic velocity field and the halo mass function, a comprehensive analysis was conducted. Initially, theoretical predictions for the halo model of structure formation were reviewed, specifically regarding linear perturbations' impact on halos. Thereafter, an examination of existing observational data from galaxy surveys was performed to determine if non-relativistic neutrinos influence the halo mass function. Additionally, simulations were utilized to assess the effect of velocity field perturbations on halos of varying masses. Then, a theoretical framework was derived to describe how perturbations in the velocity field affect halo formation. Furthermore, the analysis extended to neutrino mass constraints by investigating how relativistic neutrinos affect the halo mass function, according to simulation results. Finally, a plan was outlined to utilize future galaxy survey data for detecting relativistic neutrinos.

One of the key challenges in using atomic interferometry for measuring local magnetic fields is overcoming the minimal measurable value of the technique, especially when interacting with weak fields in a strong external field. A novel approach has been proposed to address this issue by incorporating the Meissner effect of superconducting materials, which can create a magnetic field-free zone within the atomic cloud. By positioning the superconducting material in close proximity to the atomic cloud, even very small local variations in the magnetic field can cause the cloud to split, leading to reduced interference patterns and enhanced measurement sensitivity. A theoretical model has been developed to explain the performance of this method, and it is anticipated that with an optimal superconducting ring of 10 microns in radius and a magnetic field strength of 10 G, atomic interferometry can effectively detect variations as small as 10^-10 G.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of a single Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while larger coupling led to distinctization of YSR state splitting. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. Further analysis revealed that localized spin polarization on Nb atoms is crucial for understanding YSR state behavior. Experiments on single and multiple Mn cluster arrangements on the Nb(110) surface were also successfully interpreted using the theoretical model, confirming its effectiveness.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on diagnosing skin cancer using images. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous as it contains malignant carcinomas. To address the outlier class, we employed an entropy-based approach to detect unusual samples. Furthermore, we utilized a deep learning algorithm to develop a classification model that distinguishes between malignant and benign carcinomas. The proposed method involves using a pre-trained CNN to generate features for image analysis. In the challenge, our ensemble model achieved a accuracy of 87.15% on unseen data, securing 3rd place in task 1. In task 2, our single-model approach yielded a accuracy of 83.59% on the testing images and 92.32% on the testing metadata, resulting in 4th place rankings.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Efficient Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development.

We provide a concise summary of key concepts by Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. Their ideas form the basis of our previous paper, which presented a novel framework combining first-order logic and arithmetic. Our initial report outlined the foundations of this combined system, including a recursive definition of logically valid statements, a characterization of logical truth, and an undecidability proof. In the current summary, we review their contributions that facilitated our earlier findings and lay the ground for future applications.

This paper examines the concept of invariant sets in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. A key idea is that invariant sets separate the phase space into regions where trajectories either bond together or diverge. Although this idea is straightforward for 1-dimensional systems, it becomes complex for higher-dimensional systems. In the case of two-dimensional systems, only points or lines can be invariant. This paper extends this understanding to fractional-order dynamical systems, focusing on plans in two-dimensional space. A key theorem is presented, stating that in a planar fractional dynamical system, only points or lines can be invariant surfaces unless the system's leading term dominates or the system is linear with distinct eigenvalues.

Reconstructing the source signal inside a cavity when an acoustic wave is transmitted to an adjacent structure and detected as a vibration signal, is referred to as the structural acoustic source identification problem. Despite the importance of this technique, there are significant challenges in using gradient-based optimization methods to solve this issue, particularly in a Bayesian framework, as the process of calculating the gradient is complicated and time-consuming. To address this issue, an efficient method called "Inverse Source Identification" has been proposed, which utilizes an operator that maps the source signal to the vibration signal of the structure. The proposed approach has several advantages over existing methods, including the use of a Gaussian prior distribution for the source signal and the utilization of a sparse representation framework. In a simulation, the proposed technique demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods, and it was also found to work effectively with real-data experiments.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest scoto-seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of fundamental parameters. Notably, we demonstrate that a dark parity symmetry is unnecessary for generating the dark matter mass, and that a minimal implementation can yield a wide range of neutrino masses. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between the top quark mass, dark matter relic density, and neutrino oscillation lengths, revealing several constraints. Notably, we find that a first-order electroweak phase transition is possible only when the lightest neutrino mass is extremely small. Additionally, we examine the connection between the dark sector parameters, dark matter annihilation rates, and the stability of the vacuum state. Notably, we observe that a low neutrino oscillation length is essential for both the generation of dark matter relic density and the maintenance of the electroweak symmetry at low temperatures. Moreover, we analyze the implications of our findings for the dark matter detection prospects, noting that a low-energy neutrino oscillation length is necessary for the creation of heavy neutrinos through dark matter annihilation. Finally, we examine the composite operator leading to neutrino mass generation, verifying that its impact on the vacuum stability is negligible.
